genesis2.text: “Then the Lord God formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.”

matt5.text: “You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.”

ezek37.text: “The hand of the Lord was on me, and he brought me out by the Spirit of the Lord and set me in the middle of a valley; it was full of bones. He led me back and forth among them, and I saw a great many bones on the floor of the valley, bones that were very dry. He asked me, ‘Son of man, can these bones live?’ I said, ‘Sovereign Lord, you alone know.’ Then he said to me, ‘Prophesy to these bones and say to them, “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord! This is what the Sovereign Lord says to these bones: I will make breath enter you, and you will come to life. I will attach tendons to you and make flesh come upon you and cover you with skin; I will put breath in you, and you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the Lord.”’ So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I was prophesying, there was a noise, a rattling sound, and the bones came together, bone to bone. I looked, and tendons and flesh appeared on them and skin covered them, but there was no breath in them. Then he said to me, ‘Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to it, “This is what the Sovereign Lord says: Come, breath, from the four winds and breathe into these slain, that they may live.”’ So I prophesied as he commanded me, and breath entered them; they came to life and stood up on their feet—a vast army. Then he said to me: ‘Son of man, these bones are the people of Israel. They say, “Our bones are dried up and our hope is gone; we are cut off.” Therefore prophesy and say to them: “This is what the Sovereign Lord says: My people, I am going to open your graves and bring you up from them; I will bring you back to the land of Israel. Then you, my people, will know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and bring you up from them. I will put my Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I the Lord have spoken, and I have done it, declares the Lord.”’”

merton.name: Thomas Merton

dubois.name: W.E.B. Du Bois
dubois.quote: Be ready at any moment to give up what you are for what you might become.

tarfon.quote: Do not be daunted by the enormity of the world’s grief. Do justly now, love mercy now, walk humbly now. You are not obligated to complete the work, but neither are you free to abandon it.

questions.text: Last week, Pastor Chris told a story about talking to his son on the phone. If his son could tell that Pastor Chris was distracted by a text message, his son would just hang up on him. Simone Weil says, “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” We live in a world where apps and phones are built to steal our attention, and it can feel almost impossible to fight. Think of a person in your life who deserves your full attention right now — a spouse, a child, a friend, a coworker. When was the last time your phone “won” over that person, and how did it feel afterward, for both of you?

Paying close attention to the world is not always comfortable. The pastor described watching her pet scorpion, Scout, and accidentally making eye contact with the cricket about to become her dinner — and suddenly feeling the weight of that little creature’s fear. In the same way, noticing how many shady trees line the wealthier streets of Houston, compared to how few line the poorer ones, can turn a simple walk outside into a reminder of real inequality. Describe a time when slowing down to really notice something — a person, a neighborhood, a headline — ended up showing you a hard truth you wish you hadn’t seen. Was it still worth paying attention?

The pastor’s spiritual director once asked her a simple question: “What is the purpose of a flower?” Her first answer was, “To bloom. To be a flower.” Thomas Merton wrote something similar: “A tree gives glory to God by being a tree.” In Genesis 2:7, God simply breathes life into the dust, and it becomes a living being — already bringing God glory just by existing, breathing, and being alive. Many of us live as if our worth depends on achieving something impressive, rather than just becoming fully who God already made us to be. If “blooming” is really your only job, what is one way you are currently working way too hard to be something you are not? What would it look like this week to just let yourself bloom instead?

Jesus tells us, “You are the light of the world… let your light shine before others” (Matthew 5:14–16), and Peter reminds us to use whatever gift we have been given to serve others (1 Peter 4:10). A friend of the pastor, Judy Lee, was once asked in front of a room, “Are you where you want to be in life?” She answered, “Honestly, I don’t know if I’m where I want to be, but I’m who I want to be, and the rest is figure-outable.” W.E.B. Du Bois wrote, “Be ready at any moment to give up what you are for what you might become.” Which do you spend more energy on: worrying about where you are — your job, your house, your relationship status — or becoming who you are? What gift has God already given you that you could use to “light up” someone else’s life this week, no matter your current circumstances?

Ezekiel stood in a valley full of dry, dead bones and heard God ask him, “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel’s honest answer was basically, “Only you know, God” (Ezekiel 37:1–14). Humans seem to be one of the only creatures who can imagine a future that does not exist yet — a squirrel buries nuts for a winter it can picture, but it cannot imagine a world without hunger at all. The first miracle in this story might not be the bones coming back to life, but Ezekiel’s willingness to even imagine that it was possible. Think of a situation in your life right now that feels as dead and hopeless as a valley of dry bones. If God asked you today, “Can this situation live again?” what would your honest, out-loud answer be?

Years ago, a stranger named Greg Gomez was guarding the pastor in a pickup basketball game and, almost out of nowhere, asked, “Have you ever thought about being a teacher?” That one question changed the direction of his whole life. In a similar story, a football player only started dating the woman who became his wife after his own dad asked him, “Why aren’t you dating her?” Sometimes we cannot imagine a new future for ourselves until someone else asks us the right question. Has anyone ever asked you an unexpected question that planted a seed for a future you had not imagined for yourself? Is there a question you could ask someone else this week that might open up a new possibility for them?

God did not just hand Ezekiel a finished miracle — God asked Ezekiel to prophesy to the bones and to the breath, making Ezekiel a partner in the resurrection (Ezekiel 37:1–14). This is like the old story of the preacher who refused a canoe, a motorboat, and finally a helicopter during a flood, insisting God would save him through faith alone — only to learn afterward that God had already sent the help. Rabbi Tarfon’s well-known wisdom says, “You are not obligated to complete the work, but neither are you free to abandon it.” Where in your life are you waiting passively for God to fix something, when God might actually be asking you to participate — to pick up the phone, show up, or do the hard thing? What is one piece of “the work” in front of you that you have been avoiding, even though you know you are not free to abandon it?

God never told Ezekiel that exile was not so bad, or that everything was secretly fine — God let the bones stay completely dead and hopeless-looking before giving Ezekiel a vision of new life. Real hope does not pretend the pain away; it holds both truths at the same time. At the end of the service, the congregation was asked to picture exactly where they would be at this same time tomorrow — home, work, school, a coffee shop — and to name, in one word, what they would need from God in that place. Without pretending your current struggles are smaller than they are, where will you be at this exact time tomorrow, and what one thing do you most need from God to meet you there?

prayer.label: Closing Prayer
prayer.text:
Dear God,

Thank you for the gift of attention, and forgive us for the times we have given it to a screen instead of to the people right in front of us who needed it most.

Give us the courage to keep paying attention to your world even when it shows us pain we would rather not see, trusting that noticing is the first step toward caring.

Teach us, like a flower or a tree, to stop striving to be something impressive and simply become who you already made us to be — and then to let that light shine for others to see.

Thank you for the gift of imagination. Where we see only dry bones and dead ends, give us the courage to ask, with Ezekiel, whether new life is still possible.

Help us not to wait passively for rescue, but to participate in the hope you are building — remembering that we are not obligated to finish the work, but we are not free to walk away from it either.

And God, meet us this time tomorrow, wherever we will be. Give us exactly what we need — peace, strength, patience, or courage — and help us to notice you there.

We ask this in the name of Jesus, who breathes new life into dry places. Amen.
prayer.source: — Based on this week’s study: attention as generosity, becoming who we already are, the gift of imagination, and participating in God’s hope today and tomorrow.
